content: 1. Human rabies virus immune globulin is an immunological agent approved by the FDA for post-exposure prophylaxis of rabies. Common adverse reactions include injection site reactions. 2. Rabies vaccine and HyperRAB S/D should be administered to all individuals suspected of rabies exposure, except for those previously immunized with the rabies vaccine and confirmed to have adequate rabies antibody titers. These individuals should only receive the vaccine. 3. HyperRAB S/D should be administered as soon as possible after exposure but can be given up to the eighth day after the first vaccine dose. 4. Each potential rabies exposure must be evaluated individually. Factors to consider include the species of the biting animal, the circumstances of the biting incident, the type of exposure, the vaccination status of the biting animal, and the presence of rabies in the region. 5. Carnivorous wild animals (e.g., skunks, foxes, coyotes, raccoons, bobcats) and bats are the most common rabies carriers in the U.S. Post-exposure prophylaxis should be initiated unless the animal is tested and confirmed not to be rabid. 6. Domestic dogs and cats in the U.S. have varying risks of rabies infection depending on the region. In most of Asia, Africa, and Latin America, dogs are the primary source of human rabies exposure. 7. Rodents and lagomorphs (e.g., rabbits, hares) are rarely infected with rabies and have not been known to cause human rabies in the U.S. However, woodchucks accounted for most rodent rabies cases reported to the CDC from 1971 to 1988. 8. Rabies is transmitted only when the virus enters open cuts, wounds, or mucous membranes. Bite exposures involve skin penetration by teeth, while non-bite exposures include scratches, abrasions, or wounds contaminated with saliva or infectious material from a rabid animal. 9. Immediate and thorough washing of bite wounds and scratches with soap and water is the most effective measure to prevent rabies. Tetanus prophylaxis and measures to control bacterial infection should also be provided as indicated. 10. Active immunization should begin as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within 24 hours. Passive immunization with rabies immune globulin (human) is recommended for all bite and non-bite exposures from animals suspected of being rabid. 11. Rabies immune globulin (human) should be administered in conjunction with the rabies vaccine and can be given up to the seventh day after the first vaccine dose. Beyond this period, it is not indicated as an antibody response to the vaccine is presumed to have occurred. 12. HyperRAB S/D should be infiltrated around the wound site, with the remainder administered intramuscularly in the deltoid or lateral thigh muscle. The gluteal region should not be used due to the risk of sciatic nerve injury. 13. HyperRAB S/D should not be administered in the same syringe or anatomical site as the vaccine. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration before administration. 14. Products made from human plasma, such as HyperRAB S/D, may carry a risk of transmitting infectious agents, including viruses and, theoretically, the Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) agent. Plasma donors are screened, and measures are taken to inactivate and remove viruses, but the risk cannot be completely eliminated. 15. Physicians should discuss the risks and benefits of HyperRAB S/D with patients before prescribing or administering it. Caution is advised for patients with a history of systemic allergic reactions to human immunoglobulin preparations. 16. HyperRAB S/D should not be administered intravenously due to the potential for serious reactions. Epinephrine should be available to treat acute anaphylactoid symptoms. 17. Adverse reactions may include soreness at the injection site and mild temperature elevations. Rarely, angioneurotic edema, skin rash, nephrotic syndrome, and anaphylactic shock have been reported. 18. Repeated doses of HyperRAB S/D should not be administered once vaccine treatment has begun, as this may interfere with the development of active immunity. 19. HyperRAB S/D may interfere with the response to live vaccines (e.g., measles, mumps, polio, rubella). Live vaccines should not be administered within three months after HyperRAB S/D administration. 20. There is limited information on the use of HyperRAB S/D in specific populations, including pregnant women, nursing mothers, pediatric patients, geriatric patients, and immunocompromised individuals. It should be used in pregnant women only if clearly needed. 21. HyperRAB S/D is supplied in 2 mL and 10 mL single-dose vials with an average potency of 150 IU/mL. It is preservative-free and latex-free. It should be stored under refrigeration and not used if frozen. 22. The manufacturing process for HyperRAB S/D includes steps to inactivate and remove viruses, providing reasonable assurance of safety against low levels of infectious agents, including CJD/vCJD. 23. Clinical studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of rabies immune globulin in preventing rabies when administered immediately after exposure. It does not interfere with the antibody response induced by the rabies vaccine when given simultaneously. 24. HyperRAB S/D is a sterile, colorless to pale yellow or pink solution prepared from the plasma of donors hyperimmunized with the rabies vaccine. It is preservative-free and latex-free.
